props.title: Alias Nick Beal

sections.content: **Alias Nick Beal** (1949) stands as one of film noir's most fascinating devil-bargain narratives, blending supernatural horror with political corruption. Like Angel on My Shoulder (1946) and The Devil and Daniel Webster (1941), it transforms the Faust legend into a distinctly American morality tale. Ray Milland delivers a masterfully sinister performance as Nick Beal, a Mephistophelean figure who emerges from the fog to tempt an honest district attorney. The film's expressionistic cinematography by Lionel Lindon creates a brooding atmosphere that rivals **Double Indemnity** (1944) in its use of shadows and moral ambiguity.

sections.content: Director John Farrow crafts a remarkable study of political corruption that resonates with other noir-tinged political films like **All the King's Men** (1949) and Force of Evil (1948). The fog-shrouded port scenes and dimly lit interiors create a palpable sense of moral murkiness, while the political machinations echo contemporary concerns about corruption in post-war America. The film's religious undertones and supernatural elements set it apart from more straightforward noir entries. SUBHEAD: Supernatural Noir and Political Commentary

The film's unique position in the noir canon stems from its bold fusion of supernatural horror with political drama. While films like **Nightmare Alley** (1947) explored spiritual charlatanism and **Dead of Night** (1945) brought horror elements to psychological thriller territory, **Alias Nick Beal** manages to make its supernatural elements feel organic to its political narrative. The film's influence can be traced through later works like **Angel Heart** (1987) and **Devil's Advocate** (1997), which similarly blend supernatural evil with noir conventions.
